column1: # Case corpus for hooks/process-guard.sh. One case per line, two fields:
# `deny` means the guard must refuse the command; `allow` means it must pass
# through. Blank lines and comments are skipped.
# Issue numbers here are five digits so they name nothing. `sanitize-scan.sh`
# refuses a one-to-four-digit tracker reference in anything that ships, and this
# corpus ships. The guard matches the command shape, never the number, so the
# The corpus runs in a fixture repository with no call log and no record of the
# work committed, so every `gh pr create` that reaches the gate is refused for
# the missing record — which is what lets these cases pin the matcher: a spelling
# it misses passes, and goes red here.
# Read the `allow` half first. A false refusal is what gets a hook deleted, and
# a deleted hook enforces nothing — so the cases that cost the most here are the
# ones where a naive match refuses a command that opens nothing. Two of them
# were reproduced against the shipped version by a review, one of them denying
# The corpus also carries `allow` lines for spellings the guard deliberately
# does NOT catch. Those are limits, written down so the next reader meets them
# as a decision rather than as a hole — the convention hooks/agent-cases.tsv

column2: if [ -n "$x" ]; then gh pr create --fill; fi

column1: # Whitespace is not a spelling the guard should miss: a session that writes two
# Ordinary spellings rather than evasions, and every one of them slipped past
# the first version. `gh -R owner/repo pr create` in particular is what a
# session writes when it is being careful about which repository it is in.
# The waiver is the supported escape, and an empty one is not a waiver. This is
# the pair that matters — a reason present, and a reason that is only nominally

column2: ORRERY_WAIVE="owner said to skip it, we are mid-incident" gh pr create --fill
ORRERY_WAIVE='single quotes are a spelling too' gh pr create --fill

column1: # A waiver attached to something else in the same command line is not a waiver
# for this pull request. The first version searched the whole command string
# for the token, so this recorded a row and permitted the act.

column2: ORRERY_WAIVE="this is for the echo" echo hi; gh pr create --fill

column1: # --- closing an issue is the person's act again ----------------------------------
# The refusal on `gh issue close` was retired when the record became a file
# committed with the work; every spelling it used to catch passes now, and these
# rows are what would notice it coming back.
# `create` is not `created`, and a word boundary is what separates them.
# The permitted path, which writes the record the gate asks for.
# Quote-blind: what keeps prose from reading as a command is the command
# position. Text that does not start a command passes.

column2: echo "gh pr create is what the guard refuses"

column1: # These open a pull request and are NOT caught. They are `allow` because that is
# what the guard does, not because it is right: a guard that reasons about a
# string cannot follow one through an interpreter. Both take deciding to write,
# which is where the line is drawn — the waiver is cheaper than either.
# And the cost of being quote-blind, which is not fixable without parsing shell.
# A metacharacter inside quoted prose reads as a command separator, so writing
# *about* the guard can be refused. The workaround is one flag (--body-file);
# the alternative is a heuristic that becomes a bypass.

column2: gh pr comment 303 --body "was: ORRERY_WAIVE=x echo hi; gh pr create --fill"

column1: # A backslash-escaped `|` is alternation in a search pattern, not a pipe. An
# auditor's `grep 'push\|gh pr create'` was counted as a pull request opened.
# The limit, written down: an unescaped `|` inside quotes still reads as a pipe.
# The matcher is quote-blind by design; see the header.
# A worktree is made by the harness. Plain, flagged, env-prefixed, chained and
# rtk-rewritten spellings are refused; the subcommands that make nothing pass.

column2: echo "use EnterWorktree, not git worktree add"

column1: # Quote-blind, as for the other acts: `do` is a command-position word, so this
# echo is refused. It costs an argument, not a boundary.
# Without a tracker the gated act is a branch's first push, and `gh pr create`
# is not gated: one act per mode. These run in a second fixture (`@push`) with
# no config, where `feat` is checked out and on the remote, `solo` is not, and
# `main` is the default branch. Nothing is logged or recorded there, so every
# first push is refused for the record — which pins what counts as one.

column2: git commit -m x && git push origin solo
